title: Beyond "just a Joke"

affiliation.name: Université Toulouse - Jean Jaurès
Université Toulouse - Jean Jaurès
Université Toulouse - Jean Jaurès

journal: The European Journal of Humour Research
abstract: <jats:p>This study examines how sexist humour is perceived by investigating the roles of joke target (men vs. women), participant gender, and ambivalent attitudes towards both groups. Using an online questionnaire disseminated through Facebook community groups in major French cities, we initially collected responses from 896 participants. After excluding incomplete responses, refusals of scientific use, and failed attention checks, the final sample included 544 participants. Using formally equivalent sexist jokes adapted for male and female targets within the same stereotype domain, participants rated each joke’s funniness and offensiveness. All sexist jokes focused on intelligence stereotypes. Women judged all forms of disparaging humour as more offensive than men did, and jokes targeting women were perceived as less funny and more offensive than jokes targeting men. In addition, ambivalent sexist attitudes predicted humour perception: participants with stronger hostile or benevolent attitudes towards a given group tended to rate jokes targeting that group as funnier and less offensive. Some effects also extended beyond the targeted group, suggesting that sexist attitudes may shape responses to disparaging humour more broadly. By directly comparing formally equivalent jokes about men and women, this study shows that humour reception is shaped jointly by structural social asymmetries and individual ideological attitudes, challenging the idea that it is “just a joke.”</jats:p>

title: Taurine metabolism: a potential target for neuroprotection in age-related neurodegenerative diseases
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Taurine is one of the most abundant free amino acids in mammals and plays essential roles in cellular homeostasis, mitochondrial function, calcium regulation and neuronal survival. Taurine availability varies markedly across tissues, species and sexes, reflecting the balance between endogenous synthesis, dietary intake, transport and efflux. Although reduced taurine levels have been reported in some aging tissues, recent longitudinal studies indicate that circulating taurine does not decline universally with age, and its value as a biomarker of aging remains debated. Alterations in taurine or its transporter SLC6A6 have been described in Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, Huntington’s disease and retinal degenerations. Preclinical studies indicate that taurine supplementation mitigates excitotoxicity, stabilizes mitochondrial function, reduces neuroinflammation and supports myelination and synaptic balance. Despite this strong mechanistic rationale, clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided trials and a clearer definition of optimal therapeutic windows. In this review, we summarize the general properties of taurine and its metabolic regulation. We examine taurine’s neuroprotective properties across different neurodegenerative conditions and discuss future perspectives for targeting taurine metabolism as a promising but largely unexplored strategy for intervention in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Three-dimensional missing-tooth localization in cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is challenged by partial annotation and scanner-dependent acquisition differences, while the benefit of unlabeled scans remains uncertain. We therefore conducted a leakage-controlled evaluation of physical-space reconstruction, vendor-adversarial learning, dense teacher–student consistency, and reliability-gated semi-supervision under common case-level partitions. After excluding two discordantly annotated exact duplicates, 83 labeled and 73 unlabeled scans with 111 objects were eligible. Across 75 repeated-seed runs, mean pFROC was 0.890 for pure supervision, 0.899 for vendor-adversarial training, and 0.872 for gated semi-supervision. In 50 post-lock exploratory benchmark runs, conventional 3D detection achieved 0.921 versus 0.886 for confidence-only Mean-Teacher-3D; the primary fold-blocked test was not significant (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$p=0.25$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ). A post-lock exploratory cumulative gate ablation showed no pFROC change from uncertainty alone; full gating increased mean pseudo-label precision at confidence 0.70 to 0.826 while reducing coverage to 0.680, and modestly increased pFROC by 0.007 (
                    <jats:inline-formula>
                      <jats:tex-math>$$p=0.50$$</jats:tex-math>
                    </jats:inline-formula>
                    ). After fold-specific calibration, vendor-adversarial training achieved the strongest locked outer-test operating point: sensitivity 0.793 (95% CI 0.697–0.880) at 0.458 false positives per volume (0.301–0.639). Post-lock leave-one-vendor-out results were heterogeneous: vendor-adversarial training was numerically strongest for Meyer and Newtom but not Kavo. Semi-supervised superiority was not demonstrated. The study is therefore positioned as an auditable evaluation of acquisition control and unlabeled-data use in multi-vendor CBCT rather than as evidence for a fundamentally novel or universally superior semi-supervised algorithm. These conclusions are specific to the investigated cohort and acquisition profiles and do not establish scanner-independent generalization.

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The reproductive-endocrine effects of GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) in polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS; formerly polycystic ovary syndrome) and their relationship to metabolic improvement remain uncertain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We performed a frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis of randomized trials comparing GLP-1RA, metformin, their combination, and placebo. An adapted CINeMA assessment evaluated certainty about any difference. Exploratory meta-regressions examined metabolic-endocrine associations; drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) examined genetically proxied GLP1R expression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-two reports published during 2000–2026 represented 35 trials and 2,580 randomized participants; 34 trials contributed quantitative data. Versus metformin, combination therapy lowered HOMA-IR (MD −0.91, 95% CI −1.22 to −0.60) and free androgen index (MD −2.46, −3.97 to −0.96), and increased SHBG (MD 10.21 nmol/L, 6.54–13.89). Ovulation favored combination therapy (OR 16.12, 95% CI 2.87–90.63), but was source-sensitive; pregnancy comparisons remained imprecise. Of 186 comparisons, certainty was moderate for 15, low for 21, and very low for 150. No meta-regression association survived multiplicity adjustment. MR associated genetically proxied GLP1R expression with lower total testosterone (β −0.049, 95% CI −0.076 to −0.022), lower bioavailable testosterone, and higher SHBG.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Combination therapy may improve selected short-term metabolic and androgen-related measures in women with PMOS and overweight or obesity. Genetic findings provide complementary evidence linking genetically proxied GLP1R expression to androgen-related traits. Larger, longer-term trials are needed to determine whether these changes translate into reproductive and patient-important benefits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract: <jats:p>Broadband tunability is a key pursuit for terahertz (THz) free-electron lasers, yet it is often constrained by the narrow energy acceptance of laser modulators in prebunched schemes. Here, we propose a harmonic modulation scheme to decouple this constraint. Taking the Electron Source Test Facility at Dalian as a specific case study, our simulations demonstrate that by matching the laser field to higher-order harmonic resonances of the undulator, we can obtain efficient energy modulation across a significantly wider electron energy range (40–130 MeV), surpassing the limit of 71–130 MeV imposed by the fundamental resonance. This technique facilitates continuous frequency tuning from 0.5 to 30 THz using a single modulator-radiator chain, establishing a versatile method for ultrabroadband THz generation.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Diabetic foot ulcers (DFUs) are characterized by severe microvascular impairment, where unresolved chronic inflammation and persistent oxidative stress disrupt endothelial function and arrest angiogenesis. The collapse of the vascular niche underscores the clinical need to shift the microenvironment from inflammation to active resolution. The heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1) signaling pathway is a critical endogenous defense mechanism that mitigates reactive oxygen species (ROS) and generates vasoprotective metabolites, making it an optimal target for vascular rescue. This review explores the potential strategic repurposing of classic anti-inflammatory agents, such as locally administered glucocorticoids, aspirin-triggered pro-resolving mediators, and macrolides such as azithromycin as upstream modulators of HO-1 to reprogram the hostile DFU microenvironment. While systemic administration of these drugs often delays wound healing and risks immunosuppression, their localized therapeutic potential is immense. Consequently, we highlight the pivotal role of advanced pharmaceutical engineering, specifically macrophage-targeted nanocarriers and stimuli-responsive hydrogels, designed to localize anti-inflammatory delivery directly within the ischemic tissue. By bridging immunopharmacology and advanced drug delivery, targeting the HO-1 axis provides a potential translational framework to modulate chronic inflammation and support microvascular regeneration, while acknowledging the current challenges for clinical implementation.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Existing PCOS reviews largely catalogue natural products and reported molecular pathways. This structured critical review asks a different translational question: which constituents from weed, ruderal and invasive taxa remain credible candidates when target engagement, pharmacological direction, realistic exposure and safety are considered together. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science Core Collection and CAB Abstracts were searched from inception to 2 September 2026, with CABI resources used to verify weed status. Eligible pharmacological, pharmacokinetic and toxicological evidence was critically appraised using a T1–T4 mechanistic evidence hierarchy and evaluated for exposure plausibility, methodological quality and citation integrity. Results: No positive mechanistic claim reached T3 or T4. Urtica dioica L. lignans demonstrably displace dihydrotestosterone from SHBG in vitro, but the predicted consequence for free androgen exposure in vivo remains untested; flavonoid aromatase effects are assay- and context-dependent; and several widely cited systemic mechanisms are not supported by current exposure data. Silybin exposure supports a narrower liver-directed hypothesis, whereas non-absorbed inulin-type fructans provide a luminal gut-axis case in which systemic exposure is not required. Mentha spicata L. provides a reproducible human endocrine signal but no defined active constituent or molecular target. Conclusions: The principal barrier to clinical translation is not a shortage of activity signals but the absence of demonstrated in vivo target engagement, target-site pharmacokinetics and reproductive-safety qualification. No candidate currently clears all five gates. Silybum marianum flavonolignans and Cichorium intybus inulin-type fructans are therefore only provisionally prioritized for node-specific nonclinical development, while M. spicata is a mechanism-resolution research signal rather than a pharmacological lead. The framework prioritizes the experiments needed to establish development readiness; it does not infer PCOS-specific efficacy from the existing evidence.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>We discuss several possible extensions of present studies of \(\gamma \gamma \to \gamma \gamma \) scattering in ultraperipheral heavy-ion collisions. One of the possible extensions are studies for lower di-photon-invariant masses (smaller transverse momenta). New mechanisms may show up there. This includes possible studies with future FOCAL and ALICE 3 detectors. So far, only coherent \(\gamma \gamma \to \gamma \gamma \) processes, in which initial photons couple to nuclei, have been studied theoretically. Recently, we proposed to study also inelastic processes, in which initial photons couple to individual nucleons. Without special cuts, the corresponding processes are of the order of 20–30%. A study of the extent to which the inelastic processes survive under the present cuts used for the \(\gamma \gamma \to \gamma \gamma \) studies is an interesting question. They can be of interest in themselves and dedicated studies are therefore suggested. We calculate also cross section for associated neutron production. Deviation from our predictions could signal the presence of the inelastic contribution. Finally, we discuss production of single photons in UPC (\(A A \to A A \gamma \)). Corresponding cross sections for selected mechanisms are presented.</jats:p>

Taking the Electron Source Test Facility at Dalian as a specific case study, our simulations demonstrate that by matching the laser field to higher-order harmonic resonances of the undulator, we can obtain efficient energy modulation across a significantly wider electron energy range (40–130 MeV), surpassing the limit of 71–130 MeV imposed by the fundamental resonance. This technique facilitates continuous frequency tuning from 0.5 to 30 THz using a single modulator-radiator chain, establishing a versatile method for ultrabroadband THz generation.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a current-sensorless control architecture for a buck DC–DC converter that integrates input–output feedback linearization (IOFL) with an extended Kalman filter (EKF). IOFL is applied to the averaged converter model to obtain a linear input–output relation, allowing the proportional–integral–derivative (PID) gains to be selected directly from a prescribed damping ratio and natural frequency. To eliminate direct inductor-current feedback, an augmented EKF jointly estimates the inductor current and load resistance using the measured input and output voltages together with the applied duty ratio. A common lossy averaged model is employed in both the IOFL cancellation law and the EKF prediction step, thereby maintaining model consistency between the controller and estimator. The proposed architecture is experimentally evaluated under start-up conditions and abrupt changes in load resistance, input voltage, and reference voltage. Compared with a fixed-gain proportional–integral (PI) controller, the proposed method reduces the inductor-current overshoot at start-up from 62.5% to 12.5% and the start-up time from 16.7ms to 1.6ms. For a 48V-to-70V input-voltage step, the output-voltage overshoot is reduced from 6.7V to 0.2V. The EKF yields maximum absolute relative estimation errors of 1.8% for both the inductor current and load resistance. These experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of real-time current-sensorless nonlinear control with online load-resistance estimation on an embedded buck-converter platform.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation (tACS) is a non-invasive brain stimulation technique that can modulate intrinsic brain oscillations and associated cognitive processes. Gamma-band oscillations are associated with higher-order cognitive functions, particularly those mediated by the frontal cortex. This systematic review aims to summarize existing research regarding the effects of frontal gamma tACS on cognitive performance in neurotypical individuals. A systematic search in PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus identified 43 papers that fulfilled the inclusion criteria based on PRISMA guidelines. These studies were categorized into five cognitive domains: memory, intelligence and cognitive performance, decision-making and cognitive control, motor function, and visual perception. Many studies reported positive effects of frontal gamma tACS on declarative memory, motor learning, cognitive control, and certain aspects of intelligence. However, findings concerning working memory (WM) and visual perception were inconsistent. This inconsistency highlights the importance of optimizing stimulation parameters, including stimulation site, frequency, and intensity, to enhance the reliability and reproducibility of outcomes. Overall, the current evidence suggests that frontal gamma-tACS can modulate cognition under some conditions, although effects are heterogeneous and context-dependent. However, methodological heterogeneity and variability in outcome measures limit the generalizability of the findings. Standardizing experimental procedures and conducting well-controlled studies are necessary to clarify the conditions under which reproducible cognitive effects occur.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Unused remote headroom may coexist with local overvoltage when transfer power or its timing prevents surplus energy from reaching the remote resource. This study derives a causal energy-transfer envelope retaining initial releasable energy, injection timing, and converter-mode limits. The envelope gives an exact feasibility condition for an ideal two-region system; its constant-capacity specialization separates resource insufficiency from fixed-controller violations, and a bandwidth penalty gives the lag and power-ramp capability a causal controller needs to realize the ideal transfer. A temporal network optimization retains a common storage history, minimizes persistent absorption additions, prices their location through its dual, and translates them into capacitance with coupled energy margins. In 2592 two-region cases, 670 of 2160 aggregate-capacity passes exhibit fixed-droop overvoltage, including 144 with a feasible ideal transfer, of which a causal controller with a 0.5 ms lag realizes 134. In 576 network cases, shared-equipment prefix bounds leave 59 infeasible cases unresolved. In a three-terminal resistance–inductance (R–L) circuit with finite converter–current response, a necessary voltage bound preserving the sign of the impulse response excludes 30 of 60 cases; validated ball arithmetic confirms every exclusion, the extension through the recovery interval changes none, and an available-power ceiling raises the count to 37. Cases that satisfy the bound remain unresolved until a controller is simulated. A switching-function modular multilevel converter model reproduces the averaged peaks within 0.8% at 30 kJ/MVA station energies and within 4.1% at the lower nominal energies, and 1200 randomly perturbed cases contain no exclusion that meets a safe trajectory.</jats:p>

title: When Does Nanosizing Matter for Radiation Shielding? A Physical Bound, a Test of Reported Nano Advantages and Grain-Size Rules for Glass Gamma–Neutron Shields

abstract: <jats:p>Nano-sized fillers are widely reported to attenuate gamma rays better than micro-sized fillers of the same composition, yet it is unclear when particle size can matter at all. At fixed composition and density, Jensen’s inequality makes the homogeneous mixture an upper bound on narrow-beam attenuation, so nanosizing can only remove a heterogeneity penalty. We show that this penalty collapses onto a master curve in the optical size τ=Δμd and derive a packing correction from the Percus–Yevick structure factor that agrees with equilibrated Monte Carlo packings within about 4%. Without fitting, explicit packings reproduce a 37 vol% B4C self-shielding benchmark to within 1.2–3.4% for four cross-section sets, although no measurement uncertainties are available for it. For polydisperse powders the volume-weighted diameter D[4,3] is the appropriate size measure, whereas the number mean can misstate the loss by up to 76% for geometric standard deviations up to 2. In broad-beam geometry the grain effect shrinks by 15–63%, depending on slab thickness and energy, above absorption edges mainly through K fluorescence. We then compiled 65 published nano/micro studies and tested those with paired data against bounds computed for their own compositions. Above 500 keV, where no physical mechanism permits an excess, the nano samples of all 26 studies with paired data exceed the bound by a median of 9.6%, and those of the 22 studies that pass a set-up check by 8.9%, whereas matched micro samples agree with it. This excess cannot arise from grain physics or from an error in filler fraction. Its energy independence is consistent with, but does not prove, a multiplicative measurement error that affects the nano samples. All but one of the studies that show it in a testable form belong to one network of co-authoring groups, and the single independent study shows a smaller excess of about 5%. For glass-matrix gamma–neutron shields at the loadings and loss criteria considered, only the thermal-neutron absorber requires fine grains, about 0.5 µm for Gd2O3 and 5–10 µm for B4C, whereas the gamma filler can remain micrometer-sized. These results show when nanosizing is worth its cost and motivate a minimal reporting standard for attenuation studies.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electro- and magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG) enable non-invasive measurements of gamma-band oscillations, which play a central role in cortical processing. MEG with optically pumped magnetometers (OPM-MEG) is an emerging approach that may provide increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for high-frequency neural oscillations. However, whether this increased SNR extends to measurements of gamma-band oscillations during visual processing has not been established. Here, we performed simultaneous EEG and OPM-MEG recordings in 26 participants during a visual grating task and examined visually-induced power changes in the gamma (30–80 Hz) and alpha/beta (8–30 Hz) frequency ranges. Inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC) was additionally compared across modalities. Effect sizes were quantified using Cohen’s dz. OPM-MEG exhibited significantly higher SNR for visually induced gamma-band responses than EEG (dz = 0.97). This advantage was observed in the majority of participants and was accompanied by higher split-half correlations (EEG: ρ = .88; OPM-MEG: ρ = .94). In contrast, alpha/beta power changes and ITPC did not show consistent modality differences.These findings indicate that OPM-MEG provides enhanced sensitivity for detecting visually induced gamma-band oscillations compared to EEG. Improved non-invasive access to high-frequency neural dynamics may facilitate more precise investigations of cortical circuit function.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lead-free epoxy composites containing 0–35 vol % bismuth oxide (Bi2O3) were fabricated by direct ink writing. The inks contained Epon 826, 2-ethyl-4-methylimidazole, and fumed silica. Density, Vickers hardness, optical microstructure, dimensional fidelity, and photon attenuation were evaluated using 57Co, 137Cs, and 60Co gamma sources. Measured density increased from 1.09 ± 0.03 g cm–3 for the unfilled epoxy to 3.840 ± 0.009 g cm–3 at 35 vol % Bi2O3. Attenuation increased most strongly at 122 keV. Print records showed that the 30 vol % formulation extruded at a flow multiplier of 1 without a reported printing failure, whereas the 35 vol % ink became too thick to extrude during one run. The 30 vol % formulation was therefore selected for a fitted prototype plate. The installed plate demonstrates fabrication and fit; postinstallation leakage attenuation was not measured.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We are developing a new implementation of Compton imaging
  for nuclear medicine using a large volume of stacked monolithic
  silicon sensors. In this work we investigate how the spatial
  resolution is impacted by the pixel size, an important input to the
  design of the sensors. In general, CMOS design is less challenging
  with larger pixels leaving more space for analog and digital
  electronics. On the other hand, spatial resolution is one of the key
  parameters that will impact the performance of the Compton imaging
  system. It is also important to consider the range of the recoil
  electron produced in Compton or photoelectric interactions, which
  impacts how accurately the interaction point can be estimated. The
  achievable resolution was evaluated with three interaction position
  reconstruction algorithms: one based on a Gaussian fit of the
  detected charge, and two more based on the characteristic energy
  deposition along the electron track, with the Gaussian fit
  performing better at lower energies. Monte Carlo simulations were
  performed for 140 keV and 511 keV sources embedded in a water
  phantom, with pixel pitches ranging from 25 μm to
  250 μm.  Energy-averaged in-plane radial resolution degraded
  from 9.9 μm to 95 μm as pixel size increased. The
  out-of-plane resolution was 216 μm at low energies, limited
  by sensor thickness, and improved to 155–159 μm at higher
  energies for all gap geometries investigated. The results suggest
  that pixel sizes in the order of 100 μm can achieve spatial
  resolutions on the order of tens of micrometers.</jats:p>

title: A unified modeling of X-ray and gamma-ray spectro-polarimetric data: The case of Cygnus X-1
abstract:
<jats:p>With the advent of new instrumentation, the available spectro-polarimetric measurements in the X-ray and gamma-ray domains have increased significantly. For black-hole X-ray binaries such as Cygnus X-1, a clear discrepancy between the independent measurements of X-ray and soft-γ-ray polarization has emerged.
This discrepancy challenges our understanding of the accretion process and emission mechanisms, including acceleration processes at play and the geometry of the system. We thus aim to develop a general-purpose method to model the broadband, high-energy spectro-polarimetric data.
Our novel approach makes it possible to simultaneously fit the spectral and polarization data from independent instruments in different energy bands. Measurements with widely different energy bin sizes and statistical significances are combined in a robust and statistically sound way in a single fit, taking into account energy-dependent polarization mixing from different model components.
We applied our method to the spectro-polarimetric data of the black-hole X-ray binary Cygnus X-1 in the 2,keV--2,MeV range and show that it enables us to describe the shape of the elusive soft γ-rays' hard tail with unprecedented quality and in exceptional detail. We constrained the photon cutoff energy from optically thin synchrotron emission at $( _ + - )  $. Using this value, we discuss the origin of the nonthermal electrons in the context of Bohm diffusion and synchrotron cooling. We further provide a new explanation for the misalignment of the polarization of the synchrotron hard tail compared to the jet axis based on magnetic-field helicity and Doppler boosting. Overall, our new approach offers a simple and straightforward way to apply models to diverse spectro-polarimetric data for the broader community. 10^ 2 keV</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Gamma-irradiation sensitivity is relevant to planning mutation-breeding experiments, but response thresholds must be distinguished from evidence of heritable improvement. This study examined germination, survival, seedling height, visible foliar symptoms, and reported seed production in BINA soybean7 following exposure of dry seeds to cobalt-60 gamma radiation at 0, 100, 200, 250, 300, 350, 400, 450, 500, and 550 Gy. Germination was assessed after seven days using three replicates of 100 seeds per treatment; seedling height was recorded on day 14 and survival on day 21. Reported treatment summaries were analysed descriptively, with 50% response doses estimated by linear interpolation between adjacent tested doses. Germination declined from 100% in the control to 35% at 550 Gy, survival declined from 98% to 21%, and seedling height decreased from 17.66 to 1.74 cm. The interpolated 50% reduction in seedling height (GR₅₀) was approximately 346 Gy. The 50% control-adjusted mortality point (an exploratory LD₅₀ approximation) was approximately 364 Gy. Reported seed totals decreased from 1,919 in the control to zero at 500 and 550 Gy. These are descriptive response thresholds, not probit-derived estimates or evidence of successful mutant selection. The observations define a cultivar-specific M₁ dose-response pattern and provide a basis for replication and later-generation genetic assessment.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electron‐phonon‐coupling (EPC) lasers attract a great deal of interest both for their fundamental physics and wide applications in optoelectronic frontiers. At present, the phonon‐coupled mechanism has been constructed in theory and demonstrated in a variety of laser single crystals. Nevertheless, possible EPC lasing remains unexplored in polycrystalline ceramics. Here we present the intriguing phonon‐assisted laser in Nd:YAG transparent ceramics, producing extended laser emissions beyond the inherent emission from pure electronic transitions. Benefiting from high doping concentrations and strengthened EPC intensity, the output power at 1166 nm in Nd:YAG ceramics was improved to 2.0 W with a slope efficiency of 26.6%, which is twice as high as that of Nd:YAG crystals. Furthermore, via integrating EPC interaction with intracavity‐frequency doubling, the laser spectrum of Nd:YAG ceramics is extended to the yellow region, enabling a maximum output power of 60 mW at 583 nm. This EPC effect not only provides an effective method for extending the laser wavelength in transparent ceramics but also paves the way to phonon engineering frontiers in the field of highly‐integrated optical devices and applications.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Microbial electrochemical systems (MESs) couple microbial metabolism to electrode reactions and can support the transformation or capture of diverse environmental contaminants. However, decreases in aqueous concentration and increases in current do not establish that remediation has reduced environmental risk. Building on existing reviews of remediation mechanisms and contaminant hazards, we link electron allocation, extracellular electron transfer, and biofilm activity to contaminant fate across pollutant classes. We synthesize evidence across organic pollutants, nitrogen species, metals and metalloids, halogenated compounds, and emerging contaminants. Across these classes, treatment outcomes depend on electron delivery to the intended reaction, spatial overlap between active microorganisms and contaminants, and the fate of transformation products. These outcomes include complete conversion, stable immobilization, and recovery. Parent-compound loss can coexist with toxic intermediates, incomplete denitrification, phase transfer, or subsequent remobilization. The framework’s conceptual contribution is to organize these mechanisms into a common set of evidence requirements for evaluating remediation outcomes. These requirements combine product-resolved electron and mass balances, spatially resolved biofilm activity, pathway-specific controls, and post-treatment stability. Assessment should also account for energy demand, material durability, and performance in real-water matrices. By connecting interfacial electron flow to verified contaminant fate, this framework supports comparison of treatment mechanisms and identification of bottlenecks that limit reliable environmental application.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Modern free-electron laser (FEL) facilities produce x-ray pulses as short as hundreds of attoseconds for use in ultrafast science experiments. These experiments ideally require accurate characterization of the attosecond pulse duration; however, direct time-resolved diagnostic techniques are far from being a routine procedure. In the meantime, the most experimentally accessible information about the x-ray pulses is their spectra and pulse energies. We show that the statistics of these quantities from a large dataset are sufficient to determine the average “lasing” length of the electron bunches, after which FEL theory determines the statistics of the x-ray pulses. These predicted statistics can be compared to those obtained from direct time-resolved measurements. A strategy is proposed to systematically reconstruct the average FEL parameter and electron bunch length from the measured pulse spectra and energies. On the way, we extend the analytical frameworks put in place by Bonifacio and Saldin, generalizing to finite-length, nonuniform bunches with startup from shot noise.</jats:p>

title: A review on functional nature-inspired superhydrophobic surfaces fabricated by laser surface modification and thin-film coatings
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nature-inspired Superhydrophobic Surfaces (SHSs) have emerged as the multifunctional interfaces which have a significant potential in engineering, environmental and biomedical applications. In this review, the state-of-the-art in the design, fabrication, and characterization of nature inspired SHSs has been reported. This paper is focused on the fabrication of SHSs with multiple micro/nanostructures, enhancement of low-surface-energy chemistry, laser surface modification, and thin-film coating approaches for extreme water repellency. The conventional reviews have mainly classified SHSs according to materials or individual applications whereas this work proposes a structure-process-property-performance framework to link biological wetting principles with laser-enabled surface engineering and coating technologies. The role of surface chemistry and hierarchical architecture in the effect of laser wavelength, pulse duration, scanning speed, hatch spacing and scanning strategy on surface morphology and wettability is also discussed. Various performance indicators are discussed which plays a crucial role in self-cleaning, anti-icing, antifouling, antifogging, drag reduction, oil-water separation, and corrosion protection applications. Environmental concerns associated with fluorinated materials and development of fluorine-free and sustainable alternatives are also addressed in this paper.</jats:p>

title: Effect of steady magnetic field on microstructure and microhardness of laser-directed energy-deposited Ti6Al4V/TiC composite coatings
abstract: <jats:p>Coarse microstructures, reinforcement agglomeration, and non-uniform property distribution are critical issues in laser-directed energy-deposited Ti6Al4V/TiC composite coatings. To address these issues, this study adopts a steady magnetic field with gradient intensities to assist the laser-directed energy deposition process. Ti-based composite coatings were fabricated on Ti6Al4V substrates under three laser processes with different heat inputs. Macroscopic observation, microstructural characterization, and microhardness tests were performed to investigate the coupled effects of magnetic field strength and laser heat input on coating formation quality, microstructural evolution, and microhardness. A magnetic modulation coupling coefficient K was proposed to quantitatively evaluate the modulation performance. The results show that the steady magnetic field effectively improved the macroscopic forming quality of the coatings. Surface defects decreased, and the wetting angle increased monotonically with rising magnetic field strength. The magnetic field&rsquo;s modulation of microstructure and hardness was highly process-dependent. Under medium- (1,000 W, 350 mm/min, 1.2 r/min) and low-heat-input processes (800 W, 350 mm/min, 1.0 r/min), a low magnetic field of 4.07 mT yielded the optimal grain refinement and TiC dispersion uniformity. For the low-heat-input process, coating hardness first decreased slightly and then increased continuously with increasing magnetic field strength. For the medium-heat-input process, hardness increased monotonically, reaching its maximum at 12.11 mT. Under the high-heat-input process (1,200 W, 250 mm/min, 1.0 r/min), a low magnetic field aggravated microstructural coarsening, and significant strengthening was achieved only when the field strength reached 12.11 mT. The maximum coating hardness reached 1155.16 HV0.2, 50.85% higher than that of the sample without a magnetic field. The hardness evolution is governed by the combined effect of grain refinement and second-phase evolution. The proposed coupling coefficient can effectively quantify the interaction between the magnetic field and laser energy, providing a theoretical reference for optimizing steady-magnetic-field-assisted laser-directed energy deposition.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>
                    We investigate how the effective nucleon mass and symmetry energy affect pasta phase properties and the unified equation of state (EOS) of neutron stars. The nonuniform pasta structure is described within the self-consistent Thomas–Fermi approximation, while nucleonic interactions are treated in the relativistic mean-field framework with several typical parameter sets adopted. Our results indicate that the symmetry energy and its slope are crucial in determining the onset of pasta phases and their geometric configurations. In the high-density region where matter becomes uniform, the effective nucleon mass plays a dominant role. title: Ventilation-Perfusion SPECT in Pulmonary Embolism: A Pictorial Review of Imaging Findings and Diagnostic Pitfalls
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a common and potentially life-threatening condition in which timely diagnosis directly affects management. Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) imaging has an established role in the diagnostic workup, particularly when computed tomography pulmonary angiography (CTPA) is contraindicated, or when its findings are equivocal, or discordant with the clinical presentation. This pictorial review presents a practical, case-based approach to V/Q single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) interpretation in patients with suspected and confirmed PE. Through representative cases, we illustrate the added value of SPECT over planar imaging, the impact of ventilation techniques on image quality, the discordance between CTPA and V/Q findings, the diagnostic contribution of low-dose computed tomography (CT), and interval resolution following anticoagulation. By presenting these examples, we highlight clinically relevant imaging patterns, common interpretative pitfalls, and practical strategies to enhance diagnostic confidence in routine reporting.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) can trigger hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH), but the substantial overlap between severe leishmaniasis and the clinical criteria for HLH can obscure the underlying infection and delay pathogen-directed treatment, particularly in non-endemic settings. We describe three adults with VL-associated HLH who reached the same diagnosis through three distinct pathways. In the first patient, Leishmania amastigotes were identified on bone marrow smear during the evaluation of HLH. In the second, peripheral-blood metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected Leishmania early in the infectious work-up, allowing antiparasitic treatment to begin before etoposide was administered. In the third, recurrent fever and massive splenomegaly persisted despite approximately three months of etoposide-based treatment for presumed refractory HLH, while positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) raised concern for lymphoma; the diagnosis was ultimately established by splenic biopsy and repeat bone marrow examination demonstrating Leishmania. Following antileishmanial therapy, all three patients showed resolution of fever and improvement of cytopenias, hyperferritinemia, and organomegaly, and no further HLH-directed cytotoxic chemotherapy was required after the infectious diagnosis was established. Together, these cases illustrate that VL may both mimic and drive the HLH phenotype, creating a potentially preventable diagnostic delay when the infectious cause is not considered early. Careful residence and travel history, together with timely pathogen-directed testing such as serology, bone marrow examination, and peripheral-blood mNGS when available, can facilitate earlier recognition. In suspected infection-associated HLH, identifying and treating the underlying pathogen is therefore central, while additional HLH-directed immunosuppressive therapy should be individualized according to the severity and persistence of hyperinflammation.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to validate the diagnostic performance of Identify Migraine (ID‐Migraine) in a digital cohort and determine whether substituting or supplementing functional disability with pulsating pain alters overall and sex‐specific screening performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Migraine remains substantially underdiagnosed globally, with a persistent diagnostic gap that traditional screening tools have yet to close. The standard ID‐Migraine screener relies on a disability item that may be reported differently by males and females in self‐administered digital settings. This study aimed to validate the ID‐Migraine in a digital cohort and to evaluate whether a sensory pain characteristic, specifically pulsating pain, provides a more robust diagnostic anchor than functional disability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A cross‐sectional diagnostic accuracy study was conducted among 545 symptomatic adults in Turkey (4 December 2024 to 9 January 2025) who completed a 44‐item International Classification of Headache Disorders, 3rd Edition (ICHD‐3) –based digital questionnaire. Using a split‐sample design stratified by sex and ICHD‐3 status (training
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 307; validation
                      <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                       = 238), we compared the standard ID‐Migraine (nausea, photophobia, disability) with a modified ID‐Migraine (mod‐ID; substituting pulsating pain for disability) and an extended ID‐Migraine (ext‐ID; adding pulsating pain). A positive screen was defined a priori as at least two endorsed items for all models. Models were selected in the training set and performance estimated once in the validation set.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Migraine was diagnosed in 47.2% (257/545) of the cohort, yet 204/257 (79.4%) of these cases lacked a recalled prior physician diagnosis. In the validation set (112 with migraine, 126 without), the standard ID‐Migraine missed 7/19 (36.8%) of male migraine cases. The ext‐ID reached a sensitivity of 95.5% (95% confidence interval [CI] 90.0–98.1) with lower specificity of 69.8% (61.3–77.2), compared with 80.2% for the standard model; its male false‐negative rate was 5.3% (1/19). The mod‐ID gave sensitivity 77.7% (69.1–84.4) and specificity 81.0% (73.2–86.9), matching the standard screener on sensitivity while modestly improving specificity. Sex was significantly associated with diagnostic error in the standard model but not in the models incorporating pulsating pain.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In a fully digital workflow, the standard ID‐Migraine under‐detected migraine in male participants. Adding pulsating pain (ext‐ID) increased sensitivity and reduced the sex‐related difference in detection, while the mod‐ID preserved a balanced sensitivity–specificity trade‐off. We propose, as a framework requiring prospective evaluation, a two‐stage digital pathway in which ext‐ID performs initial case‐finding and a second step (mod‐ID together with clinician assessment) prioritizes identified cases, potentially improving recognition while limiting false positives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: In women with a type 3 transformation zone (TZ3), the squamocolumnar junction is not fully visible and endocervical disease may be missed. We assessed whether p16/Ki-67 dual-stain immunocytochemistry adds diagnostic information to HPV16/18 genotyping and liquid-based cytology. Methods: This single-center retrospective study included 312 HPV-positive women with colposcopically confirmed TZ3 who underwent cytology, dual staining and endocervical curettage (ECC) at one visit; ECC-detected CIN2+ was the reference standard. Nested logistic models (HPV16/18 plus cytology, with and without dual stain) were compared using the change in the area under the ROC curve (ΔAUC; AUC = probability that a woman with CIN2+ has a higher predicted risk than one without), a likelihood-ratio test and bootstrap internal validation. Results: ECC detected CIN2+ in 56 women (17.9%). Against ECC, dual-stain sensitivity was 82.1%, specificity 69.9% and negative predictive value 94.7%. Adding dual staining increased the AUC from 0.760 to 0.863 (ΔAUC 0.103, 95% CI 0.055–0.163; p < 0.001; optimism-corrected AUCs 0.751 and 0.855). Eight of ten dual-stain-negative CIN2+ cases had HPV16/18 and/or ASC-H/HSIL cytology. Conclusions: Dual staining improved statistical discrimination for ECC-detected CIN2+ beyond genotype and cytology. This does not establish clinical benefit; the test should not be used alone to omit ECC and requires external validation.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Nano-sized fillers are widely reported to attenuate gamma rays better than micro-sized fillers of the same composition, yet it is unclear when particle size can matter at all. At fixed composition and density, Jensen’s inequality makes the homogeneous mixture an upper bound on narrow-beam attenuation, so nanosizing can only remove a heterogeneity penalty. We show that this penalty collapses onto a master curve in the optical size τ=Δμd and derive a packing correction from the Percus–Yevick structure factor that agrees with equilibrated Monte Carlo packings within about 4%. Without fitting, explicit packings reproduce a 37 vol% B4C self-shielding benchmark to within 1.2–3.4% for four cross-section sets, although no measurement uncertainties are available for it. For polydisperse powders the volume-weighted diameter D[4,3] is the appropriate size measure, whereas the number mean can misstate the loss by up to 76% for geometric standard deviations up to 2. In broad-beam geometry the grain effect shrinks by 15–63%, depending on slab thickness and energy, above absorption edges mainly through K fluorescence. We then compiled 65 published nano/micro studies and tested those with paired data against bounds computed for their own compositions. Above 500 keV, where no physical mechanism permits an excess, the nano samples of all 26 studies with paired data exceed the bound by a median of 9.6%, and those of the 22 studies that pass a set-up check by 8.9%, whereas matched micro samples agree with it. This excess cannot arise from grain physics or from an error in filler fraction. Its energy independence is consistent with, but does not prove, a multiplicative measurement error that affects the nano samples. All but one of the studies that show it in a testable form belong to one network of co-authoring groups, and the single independent study shows a smaller excess of about 5%. For glass-matrix gamma–neutron shields at the loadings and loss criteria considered, only the thermal-neutron absorber requires fine grains, about 0.5 µm for Gd2O3 and 5–10 µm for B4C, whereas the gamma filler can remain micrometer-sized. These results show when nanosizing is worth its cost and motivate a minimal reporting standard for attenuation studies.</jats:p>

title: Diagnostic accuracy of cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis in suspected meningoencephalomyelitis of unknown origin in canines
abstract:
<jats:p>PICO Question
In canines with suspected meningoencephalomyelitis of unknown origin (MUO) [population], does cerebrospinal fluid analysis for pleocytosis [intervention], compared with histopathology [comparison], accurately identify underlying noninfectious inflammatory central nervous system (CNS) disease [outcome]?
 
Clinical bottom line
Category of research
Diagnosis.
Number and type of study designs reviewed
Three retrospective case series and one systematic review.
Strength of evidence
Moderate.
Outcomes reported
The four studies included collectively reported the presence or absence of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pleocytosis in dogs with histopathologically confirmed noninfectious inflammatory CNS disease or clinically diagnosed MUO where applicable. Pleocytosis is defined as a total nucleated cell count (TNCC) above the laboratory reference interval. The first study reported pleocytosis in all 22 dogs evaluated with granulomatous meningoencephalomyelitis (GME). In contrast, the second paper identified normal TNCC in a substantial proportion of GME cases, a finding mirrored by the third study across a significant number of GME, necrotising meningoencephalitis (NME), and clinically diagnosed MUO patients. Finally, the fourth study documented normal repeat CSF TNCC levels in a single dog with progressive NME within a small sample size.
Conclusion
Cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis supports a diagnosis of noninfectious inflammatory CNS disease in dogs with suspected MUO but does not exclude disease when absent. Furthermore, CSF findings cannot reliably distinguish between inflammatory disease subtypes. Therefore, CSF analysis should be interpreted alongside neurological examination, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings, and exclusion of infectious diseases rather than used as a standalone diagnostic test.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Determining the cause of adrenocorticotropin (ACTH)-dependent Cushing syndrome may require bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS). Ovine corticotropin-releasing hormone (oCRH) has been unavailable in the United States since 2020 and human CRH supply is constrained worldwide. We retrospectively reviewed 97 adults at one tertiary referral centre (1998–2018) who underwent oCRH stimulation as the peripheral component of BIPSS and in whom the sampling result was concordant with the final diagnosis: Cushing disease (CD; n = 87) or ectopic ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome (EADCS; n = 10). Ten published threshold magnitudes and three exploratory in-sample thresholds were evaluated. The area under the curve was 0.854 (95% CI 0.681–0.986) for ACTH and 0.807 (0.593–0.953) for cortisol. All five published ACTH thresholds from ≥31% to ≥50% classified the primary cohort identically (sensitivity 95%, specificity 70%); an exploratory optimum of ≥73% gave 94% and 80%, with overlapping confidence intervals and the difference driven by one ectopic patient. Bootstrap resampling showed stable discrimination but marked threshold instability, with optimal cut-offs ranging from 18% to 80%. Adding two histologically confirmed ectopic patients with central BIPSS gradients reduced specificity at Δ73% to 75%. Applying published 30-minute criteria at 30 minutes modestly changed performance. Peak ACTH occurred by 30 minutes in 62% and by 60 minutes in all patients. These estimates apply to a BIPSS-referred population and do not support adoption of a new threshold.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Male sterility is the cornerstone of heterosis utilization and hybrid crop breeding. This review provides a comprehensive update on the molecular frameworks of genic male sterility (GMS) and cytoplasmic male sterility (CMS). We highlight how structural sterility is dictated by the ABCDE floral organ identity model, with class B, C, and E genes defining stamen fate. We further detail the SPL/NZZ-triggered DYT1-TDF1-AMS-MYB80-MS1 regulatory cascade that orchestrates sporogenous development encompassing microsporogenesis, tapetum function, programmed cell death (PCD), and pollen wall formation. Additionally, we explore functional sterility, which arises from impaired anther dehiscence and pollen release governed by regulators such as ARF6/8, NST1/2, TCP5, and ICE1. For CMS, we discuss how chimeric mitochondrial ORFs drive sterility via cytotoxicity, energy collapse, aberrant tapetal PCD, and retrograde regulation. The restoration of fertility, primarily achieved through Rf-encoded pentatricopeptide repeat (PPR) proteins, is examined alongside emerging non-PPR restorers acting at DNA, translational, and metabolic levels. The dynamic coevolution of mitochondrial–nuclear interactions is reflected in the rapid expansion of Rf-like gene clusters. We conclude by outlining future perspectives emphasizing single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-based precision breeding of sterile lines, and the expanded deployment of male sterility in agriculture.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Survival in oncology is reported to be improving, often attributed to better detection, diagnostics and treatments. However, the impact of disease reclassification is largely ignored despite the potential for bias in historical comparisons. We used the Molecular International Prognostic Scoring System cohort to estimate the effect of introducing a Myelodysplastic Syndrome/ Acute Myeloid Leukemia (MDS/AML) category to the classification of Myelodysplastic Syndrome. Survival was compared between: (1) “MDS-2016” including all patients with ≤ 19% blasts and (2) “MDS-2022” restricted to patients with &lt; 10% blasts, the latter simulating a cohort without MDS/AML. Median survival increased from 3.4 years (95%CI 3.1-3.9) to 4.3 years (95%CI 4.0-4.6) and 5-year survival from 39.0% (95%CI 36.5-41.6%) to 43.6% (95%CI 40.8-46.6%) all favouring MDS-2022. Thus, reclassification alone can produce a clinically meaningful apparent improvement in survival. Consideration of this effect is essential for interest-holders. Replication in other datasets and for other diseases is warranted.</jats:p>

abstract: <jats:p>Inspectable visual evidence does not necessarily indicate that an evidence-based acceptance rule is more reliable in prediction. The aim of this study is to measure that difference in binary object-presence visual question answering. It is accompanied with an independent object detector providing localized evidence for positive answers, and an open multimodal generator, SmolVLM-256M-Instruct. The number of positive candidates accepted depends on a development-selected threshold, while negative candidates abstain because lack of detection cannot establish absence. The exploratory pilot resulted in a new replication with 60 new COCO val2017 images and 360 new adversarial POPE questions, where the images were split into development/evaluation sets. 68.75% reference-label agreement on 240 evaluation questions was obtained using direct generation. The evidence gate accepted 39 answers at 16.25% coverage with 100.00% reference agreement, while positive-only confidence selection achieved 97.44% agreement at the same accepted count. The gate had a higher accepted-answer accuracy point estimate than positive-only confidence selection, but the exploratory difference interval included zero; superiority was not established. Also reported in this study are threshold sensitivity, positive-answer retention, image-cluster bootstrap intervals and checks on component training provenance. The results apply to just one backbone and a limited object-presence task, and do not establish semantic evidence sufficiency, causal visual dependence or general hallucination mitigation. The contribution is a reproducible diagnostic case study that demonstrates how answer-class composition and component training provenance should be controlled when assessing the evidence-constrained visual answering problem.</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Background</jats:bold>
                    : Synovitis occurs in a wide range of inflammatory and non-inflammatory joint disorders and may be difficult to diagnose using clinical, radiological, and serological findings alone. The Krenn histopathological synovitis score provides a standardized method for evaluating synovial inflammation. This study assessed its diagnostic utility in synovitis.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Methods</jats:bold>
                    : In this 18-month cross-sectional study, 130 synovial biopsies from patients with clinically suspected synovitis were evaluated using the Krenn synovitis scoring system. Based on total scores, cases were categorized as low-grade (2–4) or high-grade (5–9) synovitis. Synovial scores were correlated with histopathological and clinical diagnoses. Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS v25.0.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Results</jats:bold>
                    : Most patients were males (60%) and aged 21–30 years (23.1%). The knee was the most commonly involved joint (34.6%). High-grade synovitis was observed in 73.8% of cases, with a mean synovial score of 5.48 ± 1.89. The most common diagnoses were septic arthritis (29.2%), tubercular synovitis (22.3%), chronic non-specific synovitis (20.0%), and osteoarthritis (11.5%). Clinical and histopathological diagnoses were concordant in 64.9% of cases. High-grade synovial scores showed 100% sensitivity but low specificity (27.6%) for rheumatoid arthritis, while low-grade scores demonstrated good diagnostic performance for osteoarthritis/post-traumatic arthritis (sensitivity 81.3%, specificity 81.6%, AUC 0.81). Synovial scores were significantly associated with histopathological diagnosis (p < 0.0001).
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Conclusion</jats:bold>
                    : Synovial scoring is a useful adjunct to histopathology, aiding differentiation between inflammatory and degenerative joint diseases and improving diagnostic accuracy in synovitis.
                  </jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0173_abs_001">
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hospital rapid diagnostic units (RDUs) assess outpatients with suspected serious disease, yet no validated tool estimates malignancy risk at the first RDU visit. We developed and internally validated UDR-PREDICT, a logistic prediction model with a derived integer score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0173_abs_002">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Retrospective analysis of a prospectively maintained registry of first RDU visits (2022–2025) in a Spanish tertiary hospital. The outcome was a final diagnosis of solid or haematologic malignancy. Candidate predictors available at referral were selected by least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), refitted by logistic regression and shrunk. An integer score was derived with the Framingham points method. Both were validated by bootstrapping the full procedure and by internal–external cross-validation across calendar periods; 2025 served as an exploratory temporal test.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0173_abs_003">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of 975 analysable patients, 147 (15.1 %) had malignancy. The model retained age, sex, abdominal mass, lymphadenopathy, pulmonary nodule and bone lesions. Optimism-corrected area under the curve (AUC) was 0.719 for the model and 0.721 for the score (calibration slopes 0.857 and 0.859). Across periods the pooled AUC was 0.693 (95 % CI 0.641–0.741) and the pooled calibration slope 0.737 (0.550–0.924). In 2025 (19 events) the AUC was 0.731 (0.618–0.826). Predicted risk rose from 3.9 % at 0 points to 64.9 % at 14 points; a score ≥9 identified 9.9 % of patients, 48.5 % of whom had malignancy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec id="j_dx-2026-0173_abs_004">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>UDR-PREDICT showed modest discrimination and some overfitting. It may help order first-visit priorities but requires external validation and recalibration before clinical use.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract: <jats:p>Renal failure is characterized by systemic metabolic, hematological, and biochemical alterations that contribute to accelerated oxidative stress and chronic systemic inflammation. Paraoxonase-1 (PON1) acts as an essential antioxidant enzyme bound to high-density lipoproteins, whereas ceruloplasmin serves as an acute-phase reactant with pro-oxidant potential under pathological conditions. However, the diagnostic utility of their simultaneous alterations in renal impairment remains to be fully elucidated. This study evaluated the diagnostic potential of serum paraoxonase-1 (PON1) activity and ceruloplasmin concentration in patients with renal failure. A case-control study was conducted comprising 60 renal failure patients and 30 age- and gender-matched healthy controls. Fasting blood samples were collected to analyze standard hematological, metabolic, renal, and hepatic parameters, along with serum PON1 activity (spectrophotometrically) and ceruloplasmin levels (nephelometrically). Renal failure patients demonstrated significant hematological impairments (decreased RBC, Hb, hematocrit, WBC, and platelets; (P<0.05) and metabolic dysregulation, including elevated serum glucose, triglycerides, and cholesterol alongside reduced total protein and albumin (P<0.05). Serum urea, creatinine, uric acid, potassium, and phosphorus were significantly elevated, whereas sodium was decreased  ( P<0.05 ). Serum PON1 activity was significantly reduced in renal failure patients compared to healthy controls  ( 226.1 ± 135.4  vs. 758.5 ± 353.9 nmol/ml/min, P<0.001), whereas serum ceruloplasmin concentration was significantly higher  ( 262.6 ± 40.9  vs.  233.3 ± 37.8  mg/L,  P<0.001 ). In conclusion, the reciprocal shift in serum PON1 activity and ceruloplasmin concentration reflects impaired antioxidant defense and a heightened inflammatory state in renal failure, serving as useful non-invasive biomarkers associated with renal impairment</jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case report aims to describe a young woman with MED13L (Mediator Complex Subunit 13-Like) syndrome and intellectual disability who developed a first episode of psychosis following a prolonged functional decline. It highlights the difficulty in distinguishing emerging psychosis from baseline neurodevelopmental features, particularly in individuals with communication difficulties and autism traits. It also illustrates the risk of diagnostic overshadowing and the importance of collateral history in identifying meaningful change from baseline. It further demonstrates the complexity of treatment, including rapid emergence of metabolic side effects with antipsychotics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The report is based on detailed clinical assessment, collateral history from family and multidisciplinary input. Organic causes were investigated with antibody testing, MRI and EEG, all of which were normal. Clinical progression, treatment response, and adverse effects were monitored over several months. Antipsychotic treatment was adjusted according to response and tolerability, with careful monitoring of physical health parameters.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The patient presented with progressive social withdrawal, functional decline, and increasingly distressing, elaborate self-talk, consistent with evolving psychosis. Diagnosis was challenging due to overlap with pre-existing neurodevelopmental traits, but collateral history confirmed a clear change from baseline. Risperidone initially reduced distress but caused rapid weight gain and hyperprolactinaemia. Psychotic symptoms persisted on quetiapine but improved after switching to aripiprazole, stabilising her mood, engagement, and overall functioning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case adds to the limited literature on psychiatric presentations in MED13L syndrome. It highlights the importance of recognising subtle prodromal symptoms, carefully monitoring treatment side effects, and using collateral information to guide diagnosis and management in people with intellectual disability and rare genetic syndromes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract: <jats:p>Aortic stenosis (AS) is a progressive valvular disease with rising incidence, particularly among elderly populations. Although excess mortality in severe AS is well recognised, moderate AS is also associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Current guidelines recommend valve replacement only for severe AS or in moderate AS with a concomitant surgical indication, leaving a therapeutic gap. This review summarises current knowledge on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, natural history and diagnostic challenges of AS management, with an emphasis on moderate disease. We discuss prognostic markers, including myocardial fibrosis, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction, global longitudinal strain and autonomic dysfunction, that may identify high-risk moderate AS patients. Evidence from recent and ongoing trials of transcatheter aortic valve replacement and novel pharmacotherapies is summarised, and limitations of existing valve prostheses and medical therapies are discussed. Improved risk stratification, earlier detection of pathological changes and targeted intervention may ultimately improve the management paradigm for moderate AS.</jats:p>

                    <jats:bold>Introduction</jats:bold>
                    : Neuroendocrine tumour is a malignant, well-differentiated epithelial neuroendocrine neoplasm, supported by the presence of neurosecretory granules and a diffuse, uniform immunoreactivity for neuroendocrine markers. Neuroendocrine neoplasms are extremely rare breast neoplasms accounting to less than one percent of all breast carcinomas. The histogenesis of primary neuroendocrine tumours of the breast is not clearly defined. The diagnosis of these tumours is histologically and cytologically challenging.
                    <jats:bold>Case History:</jats:bold>
                    A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman presented with bilateral non tender breast swelling. Triple assessment was done. Cytomorphological features were suggestive of Suspicious for Malignancy (Yokohama- 4). Histomorphological features were consistent with a breast carcinoma of mixed invasive special type with 75% of neuroendocrine differentiation (NET grade 2). The tumour showed immunopositivity for ER, PR, synaptophysin, chromogranin A and INSM1.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:bold>Conclusion</jats:bold>
                    : Due to its rarity and low incidence, most of the current limited knowledge of the tumours derives from anecdotal case reports. This study aims to throw light on the challenges and diagnostic dilemma faced while reporting such cases.
                  </jats:p>

abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Aims</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seed appendages are key structures involved in dispersal and have been widely used in taxonomy and evolutionary studies. In Cactaceae, however, their diversity and terminology remain unclear due to the lack of developmental and comparative studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We combined a literature survey, micromorphology, comparative ontogeny, and histochemical analyses to clarify the origin and classification of seed appendages across the family. Nine species representing different clades of Cactaceae were examined to characterize appendage development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Key Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our results identify three types of seed appendages in Cactaceae according to their ontogenetic origin: arils, derived exclusively from the funiculus in Leuenbergerioideae, Pereskioideae, Blossfeldioideae, and some Cactoideae; arillodes, originated from both the funiculus and the outer integument in some Cactoideae; and funicular envelopes, formed early and before fertilization as a continuous modification of the funiculus that surrounds the ovule in Opuntioideae. These findings indicate that inconsistent terminology has overestimated appendage diversity, as structures previously described as caruncles or strophioles correspond to arils or arillodes, while appendages in Opuntioideae are not true arils. Histochemical analyses revealed the presence of lipids and polysaccharides in all appendages of the studied species, suggesting a potential elaiosome–like function, highlighting their possible ecological role in seed dispersal, which remains to be confirmed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By distinguishing seed appendages with different developmental origins, this study provides a framework for reassessing their evolutionary diversification across Cactaceae. Identifying potential elaiosomes also highlights their possible ecological role, raising new questions about seed dispersal strategies and animal–plant interactions. Finally, integrating ontogenetic, evolutionary, and ecological perspectives broadens understanding of reproductive trait diversification in Cactaceae and provides a basis for future studies of reproductive biology and conservation to investigate relationships among seed appendage morphology, ecological functions, and dispersal mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Behçet syndrome (BS) is a chronic autoinflammatory vasculitis driven by dysregulation of innate immunity, whereas pemphigoid diseases are autoantibody-mediated subepidermal blistering disorders. The co-occurrence of the two conditions is rare and poses a substantial diagnostic challenge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Case description</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 68-year-old man presented with intermittent diarrhea, recurrent oral and genital ulcers, widespread tense bullae, and isolated conjunctivitis. Endoscopy showed multiple discrete ulcers in the gastric antrum and a single exudative ulcer in the ileocecal region. Recurrent oral and genital ulcers alone met the 2014 International Criteria for Behçet's Disease (4 points), and a positive pathergy test brought the total score to 5. Nevertheless, these criteria are intended for research classification rather than as a diagnostic gold standard; the diagnosis was further supported by the endoscopic findings and systematic exclusion of alternative disorders. The generalized tense bullae were atypical for BS and did not respond to BS-directed treatment. Skin biopsy, direct immunofluorescence, and circulating pemphigoid-related antibodies collectively indicated that the bullous eruption represented a pemphigoid-spectrum disorder, leading to the final diagnosis of BS coexisting with pemphigoid.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This case highlights the risk of overlooking a coexisting, independent immune-mediated disease when classification criteria are applied rigidly. When cutaneous findings depart from the expected phenotype and fail to respond to standard therapy, a thorough immunopathological workup is warranted to identify a concurrent autoimmune blistering disorder.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Dark humour arising from political problems

affiliation.name: University of Bucharest

journal: The European Journal of Humour Research
abstract: <jats:p>This study delves into the reception of dark humour examples related to the Azerbaijani-Armenian conflict by applying a discourse-oriented approach to analyse instances of dark humour on social media. Focusing on a video about workers resting on the ground, which references violence in the Karabakh war and massacre, the study illustrates how users interpret and evaluate dark humour in an emotionally charged, sensitive social environment. Analysing dark humour content itself and 66 different comments, the findings reveal four different categories that dominate response patterns: acceptance, rejection, ambivalence, and meta-commentary. The findings highlight that the reception and interpretation of dark humour depend mainly on sociocultural, emotional, and ideological factors. While some users accept dark humour by normalising it, or relating it to coping and solidarity mechanisms, others reject its legitimacy because of the violation of social, cultural, moral, and collective boundaries. The tension between emotional factors and humour recognition is illustrated by ambivalent comments as a result of non-acceptance of dark humour. Meta-comments, instead, demonstrate that users not only deal with humour interpretation, but also with other users’ interpretations in order to negotiate meaning through interaction. The study points out that dark humour reception and interpretation around conflict-related themes is unstable and affected by several factors such as audience positioning, social and collective background, and personal experience, highlighting humour as a controversial, socially developed process.</jats:p>

title: Beyond the duodenum and the ampulla: addressing the classification and diagnostic challenges of jejunal and ileal tumours
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Primary tumours of the jejunum and ileum are uncommon despite the distal small intestine representing most of the length and mucosal surface area of the gastrointestinal tract. Their relative rarity, limited endoscopic accessibility and often non-specific clinical presentation mean that many lesions are diagnosed only after symptoms, complications or surgical resection. This review summarises the principal tumour-forming conditions of the distal small intestine, including developmental heterotopias, hamartomatous and syndromic polyps, benign epithelial precursors, adenocarcinoma, neuroendocrine neoplasms, mesenchymal tumours and lymphoid proliferations. Emphasis is placed on malignant epithelial, neuroendocrine, stromal and haematolymphoid neoplasms, with discussion of their characteristic gross, histological, immunophenotypic and molecular features. Attention is given to diagnostic pitfalls, including pseudoinvasion in Peutz-Jeghers polyps, dysplasia arising in chronic inflammatory or immune dysregulation settings, differences of small intestinal adenocarcinoma from colorectal carcinoma, grading of neuroendocrine tumours and separation of aggressive intestinal T-cell lymphomas from indolent lymphoproliferative disorders. Integrated assessment using morphology, targeted immunohistochemistry and molecular testing is essential for accurate classification, prognostication and therapeutic stratification. Improved endoscopic, imaging and genomic approaches are likely to refine diagnosis and management of these challenging and anatomically remote neoplasms. </jats:p>
